instruction.what: Step 3.2, the behaviours of the collection (stage 4, C2), read once every subgroup is through 3.1: which behaviours of the inner being the collection shows, DISCOVERED from the element observations of its subgroups. The input is every inner-being observation of the collection (`to_take_up`: the 3.1 findings of the subgroups and the older observations kept as inner being), each whole with its subgroups and occurrences, not the verses. A behaviour gathers elements; it is never a claim about what the behaviour is (that is stage 5).
read: Read the subgroups (`subgroups`: name, definition and the observations on each) and then every observation to take up, whole, subgroup by subgroup.

Look across the subgroups for elements that belong together: the same operation in a different mode, a chain that runs from one subgroup into another, the same party or circumstance, a role that recurs. A behaviour may be one subgroup, part of one, or gather elements from several; a subgroup may form none.
Read the older unsettled observations (`older_unsettled`) with them; each is answered only where a finding names an occurrence it holds.
Go back to a verse only where the observations do not settle the question, and say why (read_back).
write: Fill `answer.findings`. Each behaviour is a finding of the item flag (`parts.item` flag, `parts.flag_type` discovery, `kind` statement) that names the behaviour, says which elements belong together and why, and gathers its element observations by a `traced` node on each. At least one behaviour, or `disposition` none with its reason.

What relates elements across subgroups is a finding of operation (with its mode), chain (kind link), party (with the route, B:72), circumstance or role, each resting on the observations it relates by traced nodes.

Every finding also has `occurrence` nodes, with their `role`, on occurrences the observations it rests on cover (each observation's `occurrences`); an occurrence outside them needs a `read_back` entry {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_gathered`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.
`older`: answer each older unsettled observation on an occurrence your findings name (keep, restate, merge, consume, delete_neither, defer, carry).
The text says what the observations show; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never formulates the claim.
Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action RecordBehaviours -File <the answer file> (-Check to preview). The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

LayerCheck validates a stage 4 row from the tables alone: the demanded occurrences and the observations the row may rest on are re-derived; at least one live observation of stage layer-3 with its stable_key on the row; each observation's parts still valid and its item one the row uses; each live node has a valid role, a collection and its subgroup; each observation has a traced node on an observation the row may rest on; in 3.1 and 3.2 each occurrence node lies in the occurrences of the observations it rests on or its verse is in the recorded read-back; the completeness of IB-04 (not_used, not_gathered, the behaviour of 3.2); no observation restates a run of the verse longer than reading.observation_items max_verse_words_copied. A row that fails is unvalidated and its step is not closed.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route), whose meaning is cfg_behaviour_rule 72 (route-verses-hib-other-beings-data-only): A another being in its own right, B another being with the human inner being, C no bearing, data only; a verse may take A and B. A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

The study's primary focus is the human inner being (HIB). Each verse read is routed by what it shows, and the route is recorded in its observation. (A) Other beings in their own right: a word used of God, angels, other spirits or nature (non-HIB) is routed to Ch 13 "Other beings" (13.1 Divine, 13.2 Angels, 13.3 Other spirits, 13.4 Nature), read for what the verses say that being is and does; for God, also how his character passed to the HIB through creation in his image, held open (#1984). (B) Another being interacting with the HIB is fully in HIB scope. A verse may take A and B, described from different angles. (C) A verse with no inner-being and no other-being bearing is still assessed and recorded as data, and does not enter the narrative.

asks: Which behaviours does this collection show, discovered from the element observations of its subgroups? A behaviour may be one subgroup, part of one, or gather elements from several; a subgroup may form none. Record each behaviour as a finding of the item flag with flag_type discovery that names it and gathers its element observations by a traced node on each, saying which elements belong together and why; it states no claim about what the behaviour is (stage 5). Record also, as findings of operation, chain, party, circumstance or role, what relates elements across subgroups. Every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour or declared not gathered, with the reason. Where the collection shows no behaviour, record none with its reason.

the operation as an action description (who or what does what), its mode, the primary one
the chain of operations the verse links in sequence
the other party and the sequence, with the route
how it appears here: the circumstance of the verse

to_take_up.text: Thought as inner speech, often quoted as a sentence

1.9 Conscience and knowledge: "not all possess this knowledge … their conscience, being weak, is defiled" (1Co 8:7, 10) — knowledge shapes the conscience.; "both their minds and their consciences are defiled" (Tit 1:15).; "their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them" (Rom 2:15).

Law on the heart of those without the law: "They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them" (Rom 2:15). Heart and conscience are paired as the internal law-court of the Gentile.

2.5 Conscience — *syneidēsis* (G4893, NT only): *Bears witness:* "their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them" (Rom 2:15); "my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 9:1); "the testimony of our conscience" (2Co 1:12).; *Good, clear:* Act 23:1; 24:16; 1Ti 1:5, 19; 3:9; 2Ti 1:3; Heb 13:18; 1Pe 3:16.; *Weak, defiled, wounded:* 1Co 8:7, 10, 12. *Seared:* 1Ti 4:2. *Evil:* Heb 10:22.; *Defiled together with the mind:* "both their minds and their consciences are defiled" (Tit 1:15).; *Purified:* "the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself … [will] purify our conscience from dead works" (Heb 9:14); gifts and sacrifices "cannot perfect the conscience" (Heb 9:9); "consciousness of sins" (Heb 10:2).; *Other people's conscience:* "not your conscience, but his" (1Co 10:29); "commend ourselves to everyone's conscience" (2Co 4:2); "known also to your conscience" (2Co 5:11); "for the sake of conscience" (Rom 13:5; 1Co 10:25–28).; *Baptism as "an appeal to God for a good conscience"*, not removal of dirt from the body (1Pe 3:21).; fringe: "mindful of God" (1Pe 2:19) and "consciousness" (Heb 10:2) are tagged G4893. The word covers *awareness* as well as moral judgment [Claude reading].

2. Thoughts arise before they are chosen. Several verses describe thoughts that happen *to* the person: Ezekiel 38:10 has two stages: "thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme." First something rises, then the person works on it. [lexical] The Hebrew there is *dᵉvārîm* (H1697, "words" or "things"), literally "things will come up on your heart."; In Job 20:2, "my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me." The thoughts *respond to* an inner state.; In Daniel 7:28, "my thoughts greatly alarmed me." The thoughts act on the person.; In Romans 2:15, "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them." They are like inner voices arguing with each other.; So in these verses the person is both where thoughts come from and on the receiving end of them.

What thoughts are: Design: forming something that does not yet exist. H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). The faculty itself is neutral. *Maḥăšāvāh* covers both artistry and plots, and *mᵊzimmāh* covers both "discretion" (Prov 2:11) and "evil devices" (Prov 12:2). What makes a thought good or evil is what it is designed toward.; Reckoning: giving something its value or category. H2803H/J (60 rows): Human misreckoning: Eli "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Sam 1:13), "we esteemed him stricken" and "we esteemed him not" (Isa 53:3–4), Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Gen 38:15).; God's reckoning: "he counted it to him as righteousness" (Gen 15:6), "the Lord counts no iniquity" (Ps 32:2), and the nations "accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isa 40:15, 17).; To think is to judge the worth of something, and people can judge wrongly.; Inner speech.; "all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Ps 10:4). The thought is quoted as a sentence.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1 Sam 1:13).; *Dialogismos* covers both inner reasoning and outward "argument", "quarreling" and "disputing".; "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15).; Something that affects the body and emotions.; "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6; also 4:19; 5:10; 7:28).; "the cares of my heart" (Ps 94:19), and "haste within me" (Job 20:2).; A divided mind stalls a person: "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21, H5587A).; Creaturely and passing.; "but a breath" (Ps 94:11).; "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Ps 146:4).; "futile" (1 Cor 3:20; Rom 1:21).; "striving of heart … striving after wind" (Eccl 2:22; 4:16).

3. Within: thoughts acting on the self.: "my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me" (Job 20:2); "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15); "my thoughts greatly alarmed me" (Dan 7:28); "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21)
Conflicting thoughts accuse or excuse: Rom 2:15 (§9.2.3): Ch 7 (conscience)
In Rom 2:15 conflicting thoughts are reasonings within a person that argue with one another: the person does it, in himself, as an inner debate.
In Rom 2:15 the reasonings accuse the person or else excuse him: the working takes the part of a judge over the self, in either direction.
In Rom 2:15 the reasonings work beside the conscience, which bears witness, and the heart, on which the work of the law is written: heart, conscience and reasonings are named together.
In Pro 16:20 giving thought is attention with insight turned to the word: the person does it, and it is set as a way of life beside trusting in the Lord.
In Pro 16:20 what the attention is turned to is the word.
In Pro 16:20 attending to the word leads on: the one who does it will find good, as the one who trusts in the Lord is blessed.
The bed hosts both deliberate plotting and meditation on God.
The same path runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet"; meditate day and night "so that you may be careful to do"
Thinking before speaking: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out"

Psalm 119 gives one person's whole experience of the insolent: "The insolent utterly deride me, but I do not turn away from your law" (119:51); "The insolent smear me with lies, but with my whole heart I keep your precepts; their heart is unfeeling like fat" (119:69–70); "they have wronged me with falsehood; as for me, I will meditate on your precepts" (119:78); "The insolent have dug pitfalls for me; they do not live according to your law" (119:85); "let not the insolent oppress me" (119:122); The insolent wander from the commandments (119:21). Against them each time, the speaker holds the law, meditates, and asks for a pledge.

Fainting across every component: heart: "the whole heart faint" // "the whole head is sick" (Isa 1:5); Lam 1:22; Psa 61:2; spirit [H]: Psa 142:3; 143:4; "When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints" (Psa 77:3); soul: "hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them" (Psa 107:5); flesh: "my flesh faints for you" (Psa 63:1); life: "When my life was fainting away, I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came to you" (Jon 2:7) — fainting turns into remembering and prayer; Revisit 2026-09-28: In the same book, Jonah "was faint" under the east wind and asked to die (Jon 4:8). Fainting in ch. 2 turns to prayer; fainting in ch. 4 turns to a death-wish (Batch G §6).; For spirit-fainting in meditation (Psa 77:3), memory works either way: it deepens the fainting (Psa 77) or turns it (Psa 42:6). See Batch F §9.4.; bosom: "their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom" (Lam 2:12)
Inner inquiry in sequence: "let me meditate in my heart.' Then my spirit made a diligent search" (Psa 77:6). The heart meditates, then the spirit searches.

Revisit 2026-09-28: "uttering from the heart lying words" (Isa 59:13) uses *hāgâ* "mutter". The same verb gives "the heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Pro 15:28) and "their hearts devise violence" (Pro 24:2). The heart is an organ of rehearsal, and its content decides its moral character (Batch F §12.2).

Remembering and the spirit: "When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints" (Psa 77:3); "Let me remember my song … meditate in my heart. Then my spirit made a diligent search" (Psa 77:6) [H].

Heart and speech in step: "My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding" (Psa 49:3); "My heart became hot within me. As I mused, the fire burned; then I spoke with my tongue" (Psa 39:3); "there is in my heart as it were a burning fire … I am weary with holding it in" (Jer 20:9)

1.8 ◆ Fringe: "because the way is long … the avenger of blood in hot anger [*his heart is hot*]" (Deu 19:6) — a heated heart; "being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit" (1Pe 3:18) [U]; "Naaman … his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean" (2Ki 5:14) — flesh renewed with ritual cleanness; "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil" (Pro 15:28) — heart before mouth

12.2 The heart devising and muttering violence — one verb, opposite content: *hāgâ* "mutter, meditate" [lexical]: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things" (Pro 15:28); "for their hearts devise [*mutter*] violence, and their lips talk of trouble" (Pro 24:2); "conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words" (Isa 59:13); "Your heart will muse on the terror" (Isa 33:18); "those who seek my life … meditate treachery all day long" (Psa 38:12); [Claude reading] The heart's inner murmuring is the same act for the righteous and the violent. Its content (how to answer / violence / lies / terror) decides its moral character. The heart is an organ of rehearsal.; Also: "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (Psa 140:2); "in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence" (Psa 58:2); "war was in his heart" (Psa 55:21).

d. Thinking, planning, understanding, remembering: *Plans and devising:* Pro 16:1, 9; 19:21; 6:14, 18; 24:2; 12:20; Psa 140:2; 58:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17; Isa 10:7; Act 5:4; Eze 38:10.; *Understanding and knowing:*; "a heart to understand" (Deu 29:4); "understanding mind" (1Ki 3:9); "understand with their hearts" (Isa 6:10; Mat 13:15; Joh 12:40; Act 28:27); "an intelligent heart acquires knowledge" (Pro 18:15); "the heart of the hasty will understand" (Isa 32:4); *Remembering and "laying to heart":*; Isa 47:7; 57:1, 11; 42:25; Mal 2:2; Jer 12:11; Ecc 7:2; 9:1; Deu 4:39; 32:46; 1Sa 21:12; "call to mind" (Lam 3:21; Deu 30:1); "come into mind" (Jer 3:16; 7:31; 19:5; 32:35; 44:21; 51:50; Isa 65:17); Haggai's repeated "Consider your ways" is literally *set your heart* (Hag 1:5, 7; 2:15, 18) [lexical].; *Searching and investigating:* "I applied my heart to seek and to search out" (Ecc 1:13, 17; 7:25; 8:9, 16); "great searchings of heart" (Judg 5:15–16).; *Pondering and treasuring:* Mary "treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luk 2:19, 51); "ponder in your own hearts on your beds" (Psa 4:4); "the meditation of my heart" (Psa 19:14; 49:3).; *Questioning and reasoning:* Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 3:15; 5:22; 9:47; 24:38.

Parallel and interchangeable (poetic pairing): [Claude reading] The translators move between heart, soul, spirit and mind when rendering the same Hebrew or Greek word. That movement is itself evidence that the words' ranges overlap.
Led to: In Eliphaz's account: *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4); *"your iniquity teaches your mouth"* (v5).

Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

Attending is commanded in Jos 1:8 (the Book of the Law is to be meditated on day and night) and in 1Cor 14:29 (the others are to weigh what the prophets say). The negator of Jos 1:8 reaches 'depart' (the Book shall not depart from the mouth), so the command to meditate stands beside a command that the Law not depart.

The Lord's own attending is stated in Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 (the Lord asks Satan whether he has set his heart on his servant Job) and in Pro 5:21 (the Lord weighs all a man's paths). The act is a looking at a person or a person's ways by the Lord, with Job as the object in the first two and the man's paths in the third.

A second verb of musing stands in the same clause in Psa 77:12 (ponder, 3 before) and Psa 143:5 (ponder, 3 after), and the meditation of the heart is set between wisdom (1 before) and understanding (2 after) in Psa 49:3; in Pro 17:28 the silent fool is counted wise and intelligent. Wisdom and understanding stand beside the attending within four words in these verses.

Fear and evil stand with the considering in Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 (the fear of God 9 to 10 words after, evil turned from 12 to 13 after), in Job 15:4 (fear of God and meditation both hindered, 2 words) and in Pro 15:28 (the wicked 3 words after the ponder). The attention of the Lord rests on one who fears God and turns from evil; the meditation is set beside what is done away with.
In Psa 1:2, Psa 63:6, Psa 119:97 and Psa 143:5 meditation is a murmured dwelling on God, his law and his works, done by day and night and in the night watches; it is the person's own and continual.

In Psa 77:12, Psa 119:15, Psa 119:23, Psa 119:27, Psa 119:48, Psa 119:78, Psa 119:148 and Psa 145:5 the meditating is a resolve, I will meditate, set on God's precepts, statutes, promise, works and deeds.
In Jos 1:8 the meditating is commanded: the Book of the Law is to be meditated on day and night instead of leaving the mouth.
In Jos 1:8 the meditating leads on in a chain: it is so that the person keeps to doing what is written, and then the way is made prosperous.

What the devout meditation is set on, where a verse names it: the Book of the Law and God's law, precepts, statutes, testimonies and promise, his works, deeds and the splendor of his majesty, and God himself in Psa 63:6. Verses: Jos 1:8, Psa 1:2, Psa 63:6, Psa 77:12, Psa 119:15, Psa 119:23, Psa 119:27, Psa 119:48, Psa 119:78, Psa 119:97, Psa 119:99, Psa 119:148, Psa 143:5, Psa 145:5.
In Psa 1:2, Psa 119:48 and Psa 119:97 the meditation is a pursuit of its object: delight in the law and love of the commandments come just before the meditating on them.

The ground is set beside bearing and sin in four verses: sin is not borne by reason of the offering (Num 18:32), Paul could bear it no longer and sent (1Th 3:5), the sins are what the reasoning together addresses (Isa 1:18), and the Son of God appeared on the ground of the devil's sinning (1Jo 3:8). "He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. 9.3 From thought to action (Claude's reading): The verses trace a path from thought to deed: Arising. Thoughts come, often in the night (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Ezek 38:10; Luke 24:38).; Lodging. They stay and are dwelt on (Jer 4:14).; Reckoning. They weigh up and value things (Isa 53:4; 1 Sam 1:13).; Devising. They take the form of a plan (Ezek 38:10b; Ps 36:4).; Expression. Tongue, lips and eyes: "your tongue plots" (Ps 52:2), "devise words of deceit" (Ps 35:20), "winks his eyes plans" (Prov 16:30), "whisper … imagine the worst" (Ps 41:7).; Action. Hand and feet: "when the morning dawns, they perform it" (Mic 2:1); "a heart that devises … feet that make haste" (Prov 6:18); "their feet run to evil … their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isa 59:7).; The same path also runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59).

A supposition is held about another person or a state of affairs and acted on, and in the verses of the Gospels and Acts it proves mistaken or unverified: Mary supposed to be going to the tomb, the gardener, the group on the journey, Paul dead, the prisoners escaped, a ghost, a spirit, a sleep, a purchase, a vision. In each the verb of thinking states the supposition and the verse then states what the people did or found.

The supposition is forbidden, denied or withheld in twelve verses: do not think (Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Joh 5:45), we ought not to think (Act 17:29), that person must not suppose (Jam 1:7), let no one think me foolish (2Cor 11:16), let not my lord suppose (2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33), not to think too highly (Rom 12:3, twice), do not think to yourself (Est 4:13), the heart does not so think (Isa 10:7) and no thought of her future (Lam 1:9). In each the negator reaches the member itself, one to seven words from it.

In these verses the act is a refusal as the grammar states it: Jesus rules out the supposition that he came to abolish the Law or bring peace, accuse you, or that God is like an image; Paul rules out thinking too highly of oneself and asks that no one think him foolish. The refusal is of a supposition about Jesus, about God or about oneself, and is spoken by Jesus, by Paul and by the one counselling.

Where the supposition is held and acted on the act is a pursuit of its content: the people follow Mary out, go a day's journey, stone Paul, draw the sword, sail on, send a gift, give a daughter to a snare. The thought is the ground of a move toward the thing supposed.

What is held to be so is a state of the one who holds it: wise (1Cor 3:18, the wise within 2 words), religious (Jam 1:26), something when he is nothing (Gal 6:3), a prophet (1Cor 14:37), standing (1Cor 10:12), knowing (1Cor 8:2), with reason for confidence (Phili 3:4, confidence 6 before and 1 after) and thinking highly of oneself (Rom 12:3, faith 6 after). In each the object of the thinking is the thinker.

Anger, hiding and hunger stand beside the thought in Gen 18:30 and Gen 18:32 (the Lord's anger), 2Ki 5:11 (Naaman's anger, 4 words before), Psa 64:5 (secretly, 1 word before), 2Ki 7:12 (hide, 2 words before; hungry, 6 before) and Gen 38:15 (the covering of her face, 2 words after). The thought arises in a person who is angry, hiding or hungry, or who is faced with something concealed.

Affliction, suffering and crying stand with the thought in Lam 1:9 (affliction), 1Cor 7:26 (the present distress, 3 words after), Phili 1:17 (afflict, 1 after), 1Pe 4:1 (Christ suffered, within 2 words), Luk 13:2 (suffered), Mar 6:49 (cried out, 4 after), Joh 11:31 and Joh 20:15 (weeping) and Deu 15:9 (the cry to the Lord, 14 after). The thinking is set in verses of distress or of a response to it.

Searching and finding stand with the supposition in Gen 18:28 and Gen 18:30 ('find' is the condition of each supposed number), Mat 18:12, Luk 2:44 and Joh 20:15 (the search follows the supposition or the question) and Joh 5:39 (searching the Scriptures, 4 words before the supposition). The supposition is set in a verse of a search or of a condition to be found.

Sin, judging and evil stand with the supposition in Luk 13:2 (worse sinners), Eze 18:14 (a son who sees his father's sins), Rom 2:3 (you who judge), Joh 5:45 (accuse), Mat 9:4 (evil, 1 word after), Psa 64:5 (evil, 5 before), 1Cor 14:20 (evil, 2 before) and Pro 21:29 (the wicked, 5 before). In Mat 9:4 the evil is what is thought; in the others it stands in the clause of the person who thinks.

Truth, righteousness and the lawful stand with the supposition in Job 35:2 (just, 2 after), Mat 22:17 (lawful, 1 after), 2Cor 12:6 (truth, 5 before), 1Ti 6:5 (truth, 1 before), Phili 4:8 (honorable and just, 13 to 15 before) and Gen 18:28 (the righteous in the case put). The thought is a judgment whether something is right, true or lawful.

Small words stand in the units of the surfaces of this group and do not carry the sense of supposing: the connective G1161 in 1Cor 8:2, Rom 2:3 and 2Pe 1:13, G2532 in Rom 1:21, the particles and pronouns H3588A (Gen 20:11), H1931 (Pro 21:29), H0834A (Eze 20:32), H0853 (Neh 6:9), the preposition H0413 (Jer 40:4), the copula H1961 (Deu 15:9) and the returning H7725G (Mic 2:8). They are read in their verses as standalone and were read at stage 1 for what they do.

Wealth, teaching and counsel stand with the thought in a few verses: the imagination is the wall of the rich man's wealth (Pro 18:11, wealth 6 before), the thoughts are not to be cursed in even against the rich (Ecc 10:20, rich 7 after), the counsels of the wicked stand beside the thoughts of the righteous (Pro 12:5, 3 after), and the opinion of persons is set against teaching the way of God (Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14). The thought is set beside the wealth, the counsel or the teaching of the one who holds it.

What is conceived is a son in Jdg 13:5, 13:7, Isa 7:14, Mat 1:23 and Luk 1:31, children in Num 5:28, the speaker in Psa 51:5, a people in Num 11:12, trouble, chaff and mischief in Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4, and the worst against the speaker in Psa 41:7. The conceiving of a child is the commoner object across the verses.

Small words stand in the units of the surfaces of this group and do not carry the sense of conceiving or devising: the preposition H5921A in Psa 41:7, the Greek 'in' (G1722) in Mat 1:23 and the verb 'to have' (G2192) read with it, which together form the idiom rendered conceive. They are read in their verses as standalone beside the member that gives the sense; the grouping placed the whole surface 'conceive' under devising although most of its occurrences are bodily conceiving, which was left as uncertain.

In Luk 2:44, Joh 11:31, Joh 20:15, Act 14:19, Act 16:27 and Act 27:13 supposing is a belief about a present fact, taken up without testing: the boy is in the group, Mary goes to the tomb, the man is the gardener, Paul is dead, the prisoners have fled, the purpose is gained. The person does it, and an act rests on it.

The supposing leads straight into an act in the same verse: the parents travel a day and then search in Luk 2:44, the Jews follow Mary in Joh 11:31, Mary speaks to the one she takes for the gardener in Joh 20:15, the crowds drag Paul out in Act 14:19, the jailer draws his sword to kill himself in Act 16:27, the sailors weigh anchor in Act 27:13.

Where the supposing is acted on it is a pursuit of its content: in Joh 11:31 the Jews go after Mary to the tomb they suppose she goes to, in Luk 2:44 the parents go on a day's journey as if the boy were with them, in Act 27:13 the sailors sail on as if their purpose were gained.

What the supposing rests on is named in some verses: in Act 16:27 the jailer sees the prison doors open, in Joh 20:15 Mary is weeping and seeking the body, in Act 14:19 the crowds have stoned Paul. The supposing is taken from what is seen or felt, not from what is so.

In 1Cor 8:2, 1Ti 6:5, Luk 7:43 and Joh 21:25 a view is held: that one knows something, that godliness is gain, which debtor would love more, how many books the world could hold. The person holds it as a judgment of his own.
In 2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33 and Jam 1:7 the view is forbidden: the king is not to suppose all his sons dead or take it to heart, and the doubter is not to suppose he will receive from the Lord.

Where the view is forbidden it is a refusal: in 2Sa 13:32 and 2Sa 13:33 the king is to refuse the view that all his sons are dead, and in Jam 1:7 the doubter is to refuse the expectation of receiving.

In Act 13:25, Rom 2:3 and Jam 4:5 the view is asked of the hearers: what they suppose John to be, whether the one who judges supposes he will escape God's judgment, whether the readers suppose the Scripture speaks for nothing. The question tests the view it asks about.

The verse tests the view and corrects or confirms it: in Act 2:15 the men are not drunk, since it is the third hour; in Act 13:25 John says he is not the one; in 2Sa 13:32 and 2Sa 13:33 Amnon alone is dead; in Luk 7:43 Jesus says Simon has judged rightly.

In 1Cor 8:2, Rom 2:3 and Jam 1:7 the view is about oneself: that one knows, that one will escape judgment, that one will receive. Each verse sets the view against what is so: not yet knowing as one ought, God's judgment, the doubter's lack.

The view is set in the heart or mind: in 2Sa 13:33 the king is not to take the report to heart, in 1Ti 6:5 the false view is held by people depraved in mind, and in Pro 18:11 the rich man's wealth is a wall in his own imagination.

In Pro 18:11 and Act 17:29 imagination is the mind's own picture or device: the rich man pictures his wealth as a high wall, and human art and imagination form an image of gold or stone. What is pictured is not the thing itself.
In Act 17:29 and 1Ti 6:5 the false view is about God: the divine being is thought like an image formed by man, and godliness is taken for a way to gain. The verses deny both.
In Psa 41:7 imagining is devising harm: those who hate the psalmist plan the worst for him while they whisper together.
The devising of Psa 41:7 is a pursuit of harm against a person, and it comes from hatred: all who hate the psalmist whisper and plan the worst against him.

In Num 11:12 the conceiving is put as a rhetorical question: Moses asks whether he conceived all this people and gave them birth. The question presupposes that he did not, so the conceiving is stated as not done by him and the bodily word is used of his relation to the people.
In Num 11:12 the act is a refusal as the question puts it: Moses denies having conceived the people and so denies the charge laid on him.

Bearing follows the conceiving in six verses: 1 word after the member in Jdg 13:3, 13:5, 13:7 and Isa 7:14, 2 after in Mat 1:23 and 4 after in Luk 1:31; and calling the child's name follows in Isa 7:14 (3 after), Mat 1:23 (5) and Luk 1:31 (7). The conceiving is the first act of a pair or a series, bearing and naming.

The conceiving is stated of women whose condition the verse names: barren and not having borne (Jdg 13:3), clean and not defiled (Num 5:28), and in Heb 11:11 Sarah past the age; the negators of these verses reach the words defiled and borne, and in Jdg 13:5 and 13:7 they reach what the woman must not do (a razor, wine, unclean food). The conceiving is announced under a condition of the woman.

The divine and the human are named in eight verses: God (4), the Lord and Jesus, with Immanuel (3), Sarah (2), the woman and the child. The messenger or the Lord announces the conceiving to the woman, the woman conceives and bears a son, and the child is called by the name the Lord gives; the direction of the announcement does not change across the verses.

In thirty-five verses of narrative and saying (Gen 20:11, 1Sa 18:11, 2Ki 5:11, Psa 64:5, Jer 3:19, Luk 12:17 and the others) the thought is inner speech: the person says a sentence within, and the sentence is the thought, usually about what another will do or what will follow. The person does it, in the first person.

The thought held is shown wrong in the verse or the account: Abraham's no fear of God in Gen 20:11, Samuel before Eliab in 1Sa 16:6, Naaman's expectation in 2Ki 5:11, the father's in Judg 15:2, the Lord's hope of return in Jer 3:7, the ghost in Mar 6:49, the spirit in Luk 24:37, sleep for death in Joh 11:13, the errand in Joh 13:29, the vision in Act 12:9, more pay in Mat 20:10, the gift bought in Act 8:20.

Fear comes first and the thought gives its reason in Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, 2Sa 14:15 and Job 32:6; in Neh 6:9 the enemies mean to frighten, expecting the work to stop, and in Luk 24:37 the startled disciples take what they see for a spirit.
In Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10 and Dan 7:28 the thoughts themselves alarm the one who has them, and the color of the face changes: the thoughts work on the person and show in the body.

The heart, or the mind, is named as where the thoughts are: in Gen 6:5, Deu 15:9, 1Ch 29:18, Isa 10:7, Jer 4:14, Mat 9:4, Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Luk 1:51, Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22 and Dan 7:28 they are of the heart, lodge within it, come out of it or are revealed from it; in Eze 11:5, Eze 20:32, Eze 38:10 and Dan 2:30 they come into the mind.

Thoughts arise and lead out into acts: in Eze 38:10 thoughts come into the mind and a scheme is devised, in Dan 2:29 they come to the king in bed, and in Mat 15:19 and Mar 7:21 evil thoughts come out of the heart first, before murder, adultery and the rest.

The thoughts of people are what the Lord knows, searches and discerns: in Psa 94:11, Psa 139:2, Psa 139:23, 1Ch 28:9, 1Cor 3:20, Eze 11:5 and Isa 66:18 he knows them, and in Heb 4:12 the word discerns them with the heart's intentions. The thoughts lie open to him.
In Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8 and Luk 11:17 Jesus knows or perceives the thoughts of those around him and answers them: their thoughts are what his knowing reaches.
In 1Cor 2:11 only the spirit of a person, within him, knows his thoughts, and in Ecc 10:20 even what is cursed in thought may be carried abroad: the thought is inward and yet not hidden.

The Lord himself thinks: his thoughts toward his people are many and deep in Psa 40:5 and Psa 92:5, precious to the psalmist in Psa 139:17, above man's in Isa 55:8 and Isa 55:9 and unknown to the nations in Mic 4:12; he thought to give Israel a land in Jer 3:19, he will do to Israel as he thought to do to the nations in Num 33:56, and he takes thought for the poor in Psa 40:17.

What the thoughts are set on is evil in Gen 6:5, Job 21:27, Psa 56:5, Psa 64:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 59:7, Jer 4:14, Eze 38:10, Mat 9:4, Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21 and Jam 2:4: wrong against another, iniquity, an evil scheme, judging with evil.
In Isa 55:7 the unrighteous man is called to forsake his thoughts, and in Jer 4:14 Jerusalem is asked how long wicked thoughts will lodge within her: the thoughts are to be given up.
In Isa 55:7 forsaking the thoughts leads on: the man returns to the Lord, who has compassion and pardons abundantly.

Thinking is planning or intending in Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, 1Sa 18:25, Job 6:26, 2Ch 13:8, 2Sa 21:16 and Phili 1:17: to destroy nations, to make the people forget the name, to change times and law, to make David fall, to withstand the Lord's kingdom, to kill David, to afflict Paul. The person intends an act.

The thought is carried into the deed in the same verse: in Num 33:56 the Lord will do as he thought, in 1Sa 18:21 Saul gives his daughter as a snare, in Gen 32:20 Jacob sends the present to appease Esau, and in 1Sa 27:11 David leaves none alive.

Giving thought is attention of the mind turned to a matter: the psalmist thinks on his ways in Psa 119:59, recalls the Lord's rules in Psa 119:52, dwells on his steadfast love in Psa 48:9, and tries to understand in Psa 73:16; the prudent and the upright give thought to their steps in Pro 14:15 and Pro 21:29; the people of faith did not keep the land in mind in Heb 11:15.

Attention leads on: in Psa 119:59 thinking on his ways turns the psalmist's feet to the testimonies, in Psa 119:52 thinking of the rules brings comfort, in Psa 73:16 the thinking wearies until he goes into the sanctuary, and in Heb 11:15 keeping the land in mind would have given the chance to return.
In Phili 4:8 the thinking is commanded and given its objects: whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely and worthy of praise.
In Lam 1:9 Jerusalem took no thought of her future, and her fall followed; in Ecc 9:10 there is no thought in Sheol. The want of thought is named as a lack.

Thinking is a judgment of what is so or fitting: Judah takes the woman for a prostitute in Gen 38:15, a thing is unclean to the one who counts it so in Rom 14:14, the raising of the dead is judged incredible in Act 26:8, Paul judges what is needful in 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25, and what seems best in someone's eyes decides in Num 36:6, 2Sa 3:19, Jer 40:4 and Jer 40:5.

The thought is turned on oneself: in 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 10:12, 1Cor 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4, Jam 1:26 and Luk 8:18 a person thinks he is wise, stands, is a prophet, is something, has grounds for confidence, is religious or has what he has; in Rom 12:3 one is not to think of oneself more highly than one ought.

In Gal 6:3, Jam 1:26 and 1Cor 3:18 the self-view leads to self-deceit: the one who rates himself as something, being nothing, misleads himself, and the one who counts himself wise must first become a fool.

The thought is asked of the hearer in Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56, Luk 13:2, Luk 13:4, Heb 10:29, 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5: what do you think, do you think. The question draws out a judgment the hearer forms.

The thought is forbidden or denied in Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Joh 5:45, Act 17:29, 2Cor 11:16, Est 4:13 and Isa 10:7: do not think, we ought not to think, let no one think, do not think to yourself, his heart does not so think. The verse corrects what would be thought.

Where the thought is set against God it is a refusal: in Psa 10:4 the wicked man's thoughts say there is no God, in Rom 1:21 those who knew God did not honor or thank him and became futile in thinking, in Psa 50:21 they thought God like themselves, in Eze 20:32 the thought is to be like the nations, and in 2Cor 10:5 every lofty opinion against the knowledge of God is pulled down.

Where the thought is turned toward God it is a pursuit: in Psa 139:23 the psalmist asks God to search and know his thoughts, in Psa 139:17 God's thoughts are precious to him, in Psa 48:9 the people dwell on his steadfast love, in 1Ch 29:18 David asks that such purposes be kept in the hearts of the people, and in Psa 119:59 the thinking turns the feet to the testimonies.

The thinking has a measure: mature or childish in 1Cor 14:20 and 1Cor 13:11, sober in Rom 12:3, the same mind or another in Phili 3:15, futile in Rom 1:21, and armed with Christ's mind in 1Pe 4:1. The words give the thinking its maturity or its emptiness.

In 2Cor 10:5 the thoughts are taken captive to obey Christ, and in 2Cor 11:3 Paul fears they will be led astray from devotion to him by deceit: the thoughts are what is either brought under Christ or drawn away.
In Job 32:6, Job 32:10 and Job 32:17 Elihu holds back his opinion out of fear and then declares it, and in Pro 18:2 the fool delights only in airing his: the view is held and spoken.

In Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4 what is conceived within is then born: trouble, chaff and mischief conceived, evil, stubble and iniquity brought forth. The figure joins what is formed within to what comes out.
Faith reckons: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead"

People value and regard: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners?" (Gen 31:15); "Let not my lord hold me guilty" (2Sa 19:19); "who have no regard for silver" (Isa 13:17); "there is no regard for man" (Isa 33:8); "they were considered reliable" (Neh 13:13); God's laws "would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hos 8:12); "The precious sons of Zion" "how they are regarded as earthen pots" (Lam 4:2); "will be counted as cursing" (Pro 27:14). And a person is regarded: "we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psa 44:22); "I am counted among those who go down to the pit" (Psa 88:4); Israel "not counting itself among the nations" (Num 23:9).
The righteous regard animal life: "Whoever is righteous has regard for the life [*nephesh*] of his beast" (Pro 12:10).

Blameless soul-life: "I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life" (Job 9:21) — integrity with self-rejection; "Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright" (Pro 29:10).

b. Greek *sarx*: *Neutral uses continue:* one flesh; all flesh; "the Word became flesh" (Joh 1:14); "in the days of his flesh" (Heb 5:7); "flesh and blood" (Heb 2:14; Mat 16:17); "a thorn … in the flesh" (2Co 12:7); "our bodies had no rest … fighting without and fear within" (2Co 7:5).; *Pauline and Petrine ethical flesh — flesh as an inner orientation:*; "the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes" (1Jo 2:16); "the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind" (Eph 2:3); "the works of the flesh" (Gal 5:19); "crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (Gal 5:24); "nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out" (Rom 7:18); "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin" (Rom 7:25); "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God" (Rom 8:7); "sensuous mind" = mind of the flesh (Col 2:18) [lexical]; "confidence in the flesh" (Phili 3:3–4); "boast according to the flesh" (2Co 11:18); "judge according to the flesh" (Joh 8:15); "regard no one according to the flesh" (2Co 5:16); "plans according to the flesh" (2Co 1:17); [Claude reading] Flesh here is no longer just the body. It is a way the inner person is *oriented*, with its own desires and "mind".

The stirred person still acts as himself. Cyrus makes a proclamation and writes it down. The Medes *"have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold"* (Isa 13:17), and Cyrus works *"not for price or reward"* (45:13). Both stirred agents are men who cannot be bought. I read that God stirs a spirit already suited to the task. The verses do not say whether the stirring makes it so.

Hiding from God: In each scene where a person hides from God, something of God is perceived first: a sound (Genesis 3:10), God naming himself (Exodus 3:6), "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).; Adam hid because he knew he was naked (Genesis 3:10).; Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6), and no wrong is named.; At the end, people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us'", for "who can stand?" (Revelation 6:16–17).; Job names the one condition on which he will not hide: "Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me" (Job 13:20–21). In his words, it is the dread that makes a person hide.; None of it works. "Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jeremiah 23:24). "There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves" (Job 34:22). Isaiah names what the attempt does: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay" (Isaiah 29:15–16).; That nothing is hidden from God is the same fact for everyone, and it falls very differently.; For the one who suffers it is comfort: "O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" (Psalm 38:9).; For the one being made it is wonder: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret" (Psalm 139:15), and the psalmist answers, "my soul knows it very well" (139:14).; For the one who has done wrong it is judgement: "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore" (Hosea 5:3).

Where it comes from: the attempt to hide. "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?'" (Isa 29:15). The next verse names what that attempt does: "You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay …?" (29:16). Hiding from God inverts creature and creator.
People valuing: *"we esteemed him not"* (Isa 53:3); *"those who feared the Lord … esteemed his name"* (Mal 3:16); *"no regard for silver"* (Isa 13:17); *"there is no regard for man"* (Isa 33:8)
Being regarded: *"we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered"* (Psa 44:22) and *"I am counted among those who go down to the pit"* (Psa 88:4).

A resolve reached after weighing, then turned. *"her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly"* (Mat 1:19). The next verse: *"But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (1:20). The resolve was still being weighed, and God redirected it.

Joseph. *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Mat 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, he resolved, and he went on considering. Then God spoke into the considering.
Face: Reckoning set aside by trust; Verses: 2Ki 12:15; 22:7; Neh 13:13; What differs: "they dealt honestly"; "considered reliable"; Why (basis): Where there is honesty, the count is not asked for (S)

A word of contempt stands in the same sentence as the regard in Isa 33:8 (despised, 2 before), Act 28:22 (spoken against, 9 after) and 1Ti 6:1 (reviled, 11 after). The regard is set in a verse that also names the low standing of a city, a sect or a name.

The surface 'regard' also holds the prepositional idiom 'with regard to' in Act 28:22 (G4012), Col 2:16 (G3313), Ecc 3:18 (H1700) and Jdg 15:3 (H9006): these are not an act of taking account of anyone and are read in their verses as standalone. The negators H0408 and H3808 in Exo 5:9 and Job 9:21 are aligned into the unit of the surface and are read as negators, not as acts of regard.

The surface 'weighing' is a weight in Gen 24:22 (twice), Jos 7:21 and Eze 5:1, a measure of shekels and not an act of the mind, and the surface 'weigh' is a physical weighing out in Ezr 8:29 and Zep 1:11 (laden); 'taking' stands beside the weights in the first three (took, 2 to 4 words). These occurrences are read as standalone: they are in the group because the surface also carries an evaluative use (1Cor 14:29, Ecc 12:9), and their placement was left as uncertain in the grouping.

In Pro 24:32, Ecc 2:11, Eze 18:28, Dan 7:8, Rom 4:19 and Mat 1:20 considering is attention set on a matter and taken in: the field looked over, the toil surveyed, the transgressions seen, the horns watched, the body faced, the things Joseph turned over. The person does it, and it comes before a turn, a verdict or a word from God.
In Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 the Lord asks Satan whether he has set his heart on Job: the considering is put as a question to another, and the heart is named as what is set on the person.
In Isa 53:8 the question who of his generation considered that he was cut off states that none gave it thought: the considering is denied of the servant's own generation.
In Eze 18:28 the considering leads a chain: the man considers, turns away from the transgressions he committed, and shall live and not die.
In Pro 24:32 the considering stands between seeing and being taught: the man sees the field, sets his heart on it, looks, and receives instruction.
In Ecc 2:11 the considering of all the work and toil ends in a verdict: all was vanity and nothing was gained.

Counting someone or something as a certain thing is the second act of the subgroup: in Heb 11:11, Heb 11:19, Heb 11:26, Pro 17:28, Neh 13:13, 2Ch 9:20, Mar 10:42, Luk 22:24, Gen 31:15, Psa 44:22, Rom 8:36, Lam 4:2 and Hos 8:12 a person, a people, a thing or God is counted faithful, able, greater, wise, reliable, nothing, rulers, the greatest, foreigners, sheep, pots or strange. It is a valuation that gives a standing.

In Heb 11:11, Heb 11:19, Heb 11:26 and Rom 4:19 the counting is done by faith and is set on God: the one who promised is counted faithful, God is counted able to raise the dead, reproach for Christ is counted above Egypt's treasures with the eye on the reward, and Abraham faces his own body without his faith weakening.

In Jer 24:5, Isa 29:17 and Rom 2:26 the counting is foreseen: the Lord will count the exiles good, the field shall be counted a forest, the uncircumcised who keeps the precepts will be counted as circumcised.

The counting is commanded or asked of people in Lev 19:23, 1Ti 6:1, 1Cor 4:1, 2Th 3:15, 1Sa 1:16 and 1Sa 25:25: fruit to be counted forbidden, masters worthy of honor, the apostles as servants of Christ, the disobedient not an enemy, Hannah not a worthless woman, Nabal not to be taken to heart.

Regard is given as a done act in 2Ki 3:14, Pro 12:10 and Psa 144:3: Elisha's regard for Jehoshaphat, the righteous man's knowing care for the life of his beast, and the Lord's regard for man, which the psalmist wonders at.

Regard is asked in Psa 74:20, Psa 80:14, 2Ch 6:19 and Psa 119:117: the Lord is asked to have regard for the covenant, the vine and his servant's prayer, and the psalmist asks to be held up so that he may have regard for the statutes. In Deu 9:27 the Lord is asked not to regard the people's stubbornness.

Regard withheld is a refusal in Gen 4:5, Job 35:13, Job 37:24, Lam 4:16, Psa 28:5, Isa 5:12, Job 34:27, Deu 33:9, Job 9:21, Isa 13:17, Isa 33:8, Exo 5:9 and 1Ki 10:21: God withholds it from Cain's offering, an empty cry, the conceited and a scattered people; people withhold it from God's works and ways; Levi from his kin, Job from himself, the Medes from silver, the land from man, the men from lying words, and Solomon's days from silver. The negator reaches the regard each time.

Where regard is given or sought it is a pursuit of its object: in Pro 12:10 the righteous reaches to the life of his beast, in 2Ki 3:14 Elisha acts for the king's sake, in Psa 119:117 the psalmist seeks lasting regard for the statutes, and in 2Ch 6:19 the Lord is asked to turn to the prayer.

In 1Sa 1:16, 1Sa 25:25 and Job 37:24 the regard is bound to worth: Hannah asks not to be counted worthless, Abigail asks that worthless Nabal not be taken to heart, and God withholds regard from the wise in their own conceit.
In 2Ch 6:19 and Job 35:13 regard goes with hearing: the Lord is asked to regard the prayer and listen to the cry, and an empty cry God neither hears nor regards.
In Job 34:27 turning aside from following God and having no regard for his ways are one fault, and in Psa 28:5 not regarding the Lord's works leads to being torn down and not built up.
In Deu 33:9 withholding regard from father and mother, disowning brothers and ignoring children stands with keeping the word and the covenant: the refusal is for the sake of what is kept.
In 2Cor 5:16 the regard by the standard of the flesh is given up: Paul once knew Christ that way and now takes account of no one by it.
In 1Cor 14:29 weighing in the mind is commanded: when two or three prophets have spoken, the others are to weigh what is said, judging and discerning it.
In Ecc 12:9 the wise Preacher weighs proverbs, with studying and arranging, as part of teaching the people knowledge: the weighing tests and orders what is learned.
